summary: Download a free pediatric well-child visit note template, see a completed example, and learn how to document screenings, growth, vaccines & guidance right.
body_markdown:
A pediatric well-child visit note template gives clinicians a fixed structure for documenting the components every preventive visit must cover: interval history, growth with percentiles, developmental surveillance, standardized screenings, immunizations, and anticipatory guidance. Unlike a sick-visit SOAP note, the checklist changes with the child's age, and the note has to prove that each age-indicated item was actually done.


Below you'll find a free downloadable template, a completed worked example, an age-by-age documentation guide, and the specific habits that keep well-child notes clean for both clinical review and payer audits.


**Quick download:** Grab the free[Pediatric Well-Child Visit Note Template PDF](https://www.sully.ai/templates/pediatric-well-child-visit-note) here.


## Key Takeaways


-


**The visit has a fixed, age-specific checklist:** Well-child documentation follows the[Bright Futures/AAP periodicity schedule](https://www.aap.org/en/practice-management/bright-futures/) , so the expected components (screenings, measurements, guidance topics) change at every visit age. A good template surfaces the right items for the right age.


-


**Screenings need an instrument and a score:** "Development normal" is surveillance, not screening. To count clinically, and to be separately reportable to most payers, the note must name the standardized tool (ASQ-3, M-CHAT-R/F, PHQ-A) and record the result.


-


**Growth means percentiles, not raw numbers:** A weight of 11.2 kg tells the next clinician nothing on its own. Chart weight, length/height, head circumference, and BMI as percentiles, and interpret the trend across visits.


-


**A structured template protects the claim:** Preventive codes are age-based, screening codes require a named tool with a documented result, and vaccine administration is counted per component. A prompted template, or an[AI scribe that drafts the note for you](https://www.sully.ai/agents/scribe) , captures all three without slowing the visit down.


## What Is a Pediatric Well-Child Visit Note Template?


A pediatric well-child visit note template is a structured clinical note used to document routine health supervision visits, from the newborn visit through the adolescent years. It organizes the encounter into the standard preventive-care components: interval history, nutrition and sleep, developmental surveillance and screening, growth parameters, physical exam, age-indicated screenings, immunizations, anticipatory guidance, and the assessment and plan.


The reason it exists as a separate template, rather than just another SOAP note, is that a well visit is defined by what's *expected* , not by what the patient complains of. A 4-year-old's visit must include vision screening; an 18-month visit must include autism screening; an adolescent visit must include depression screening and a confidential interview. Miss the item, or document it vaguely, and the visit is clinically incomplete and often unbillable at the level delivered.


Think of the template as the periodicity schedule turned into a note. If it wasn't written down (the tool used, the score, the percentile, the vaccine counseling), it didn't happen.


## What to Include in a Well-Child Visit Note


After the newborn visit, the same core sections show up in every complete well-child note. Our free template is organized around them:


-


**Visit age and context:** Chronologic age, visit type (2-month, 18-month, 5-year, adolescent), and the caregiver's or patient's agenda for today.


-


**Interval history:** Illnesses, ED visits, hospitalizations, specialist care, medication and allergy updates since the last visit.


-


**Nutrition, elimination, and sleep:** Feeding pattern appropriate to age (breast/formula/solids), appetite, stooling and voiding, sleep duration, and safe-sleep practices for infants.


-


**Development, behavior, and school:** Milestone surveillance at every visit, plus formal standardized screening at the scheduled ages, with the instrument named and the score recorded.


-


**Social history and safety:** Household composition, childcare or school, tobacco and smoke exposure, food and housing security, and age-appropriate injury prevention topics (car seats, water, firearms, screens, helmets).


-


**Growth and physical exam:** Weight, length/height, head circumference (through 24 months), BMI (from age 2), blood pressure (from age 3), all with percentiles and interpretation, plus a complete age-appropriate exam.


-


**Screenings:** Vision, hearing, anemia, lead, dyslipidemia, depression, and other age-indicated screens, each documented as performed, ordered, or deferred.


-


**Immunizations:** Vaccines due per the[CDC child and adolescent immunization schedule](https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/hcp/imz-schedules/child-adolescent-age.html) , administered today, deferred, or refused with counseling documented.


-


**Anticipatory guidance:** The specific age-appropriate topics actually discussed, not a generic "guidance provided."


-


**Assessment and plan:** Health supervision visit with growth and development assessment, any problems addressed, referrals, and the return interval.


This is where a template earns its keep. A blank note invites "well child, doing well, vaccines given." A prompted template asks for the ASQ-3 communication score, the weight-for-length percentile, and which guidance topics you covered, before the family has left the room and the detail is gone.


**Pro tip:** Structure your screening section as a table with a column for the instrument and a column for the score. It's the single change that most improves both the clinical quality and the auditability of well-child notes.


## Well-Child Documentation by Age: What Changes When


The core sections stay constant; the required contents rotate. Here's what the note needs to prove at each stage:


**Age band**


**Growth documentation**


**Key screenings to document**


**Guidance priorities**


**Infant (0–12 mo)**


Weight, length, head circumference with percentiles


Maternal depression (1, 2, 4, 6 mo), developmental screening at 9 mo


Safe sleep, feeding transitions, home safety


**Toddler (12–36 mo)**


Add weight-for-length; HC through 24 mo


Developmental screening at 18 & 30 mo; autism (M-CHAT-R/F) at 18 & 24 mo; lead risk


Language exposure, screen time, car seats, dental home


**School-age (3–11 yr)**


BMI percentile from age 2; BP from age 3


Vision and hearing at scheduled ages; behavioral/social-emotional at every visit


School readiness and performance, activity, nutrition, water and bike safety


**Adolescent (12–21 yr)**


BMI percentile, BP


Depression and suicide risk annually (PHQ-A or similar); substance use (CRAFFT); STI/HIV as indicated


Confidential interview, mood, substances, sexual health, driving


The note should make the age-band logic visible: a reviewer looking at an 18-month note should immediately find the autism screen with its result, just as an adolescent note should show the depression screen and confirm the confidential interview happened.


## Pediatric Well-Child Visit Note Example


Here's how a routine visit lands in this structure. (All patient details are fictitious.)


**Visit Age / Context:** 18-month well-child visit. Caregiver concern: limited words (~5 single words), picky eating.


**Interval History:** One episode of otitis media treated with amoxicillin, resolved. No ED visits or hospitalizations. No medications. NKDA.


**Nutrition / Sleep:** Eats table foods, drinks whole milk 16 oz/day from a cup. Selective with vegetables; growth reassuring. Sleeps 11 hours overnight plus one nap.


**Development / Screening:** Walks well, stacks blocks, points to request, parallel play. ASQ-3 completed by caregiver: communication domain in monitoring zone; all other domains above cutoff. M-CHAT-R/F score 1, negative.


**Growth / Exam:** Weight 11.2 kg (45th percentile), length 81 cm (40th percentile), head circumference 47 cm (50th percentile). Weight-for-length proportionate. Complete exam normal, including dentition, gait, and TMs.


**Screenings / Immunizations:** Lead and anemia risk assessment low risk; hemoglobin ordered per clinic protocol. DTaP #4 and Hep A #1 administered today after counseling; VIS provided.


**Anticipatory Guidance:** Discussed language-rich interaction and reading daily, limiting solitary screen time, structured food exposures without pressure, car seat rear-facing, water and stair safety.


**Assessment / Plan:** Healthy 18-month-old with borderline expressive language. Referral placed to early intervention for speech evaluation. Discussed dental home. Return at 24-month well visit, sooner for illness or concerns.


Notice what makes this note audit-proof: every screen has a named instrument and a result, every growth parameter has a percentile, and the guidance section lists the topics actually covered.


## How to Write a Strong Well-Child Note: 5 Habits


A template gives you the skeleton. These habits turn it into documentation that holds up clinically and financially.


### 1. Name the instrument and record the score


Developmental *surveillance* happens at every visit; standardized *screening* happens at scheduled ages, and the two are documented differently. "Development appropriate" covers surveillance. For screening, write the tool and the result: "ASQ-3 at 18 months: communication monitoring zone, all other domains above cutoff." A non-standardized screen generally isn't separately reportable, so this one line is often the difference between a paid screening code and a denial.


### 2. Chart percentiles and interpret the trend


Raw measurements without context are noise. Record each parameter with its percentile and add one line of interpretation: "tracking along the 40th–50th percentiles, proportionate growth." If a child crosses percentile lines, say so and say what you're doing about it. That single sentence is what separates growth *monitoring* from growth *data entry* .


### 3. List the guidance topics you actually discussed


"Anticipatory guidance provided" is the weakest line in pediatric documentation. Payers and reviewers expect visit-appropriate topics, and families deserve a record of what was covered. Listing four or five specifics (safe sleep, feeding, car seat orientation, screen time) takes ten seconds with a prompted template.


### 4. Document vaccine decisions completely


For vaccines given, capture what was administered and that counseling occurred with VIS provided; lot and site per your clinic workflow. For deferrals and refusals, document the counseling conversation and the plan to revisit. Remember that immunization administration is coded per component, not per injection; a combination vaccine changes the claim.


### 5. Keep the acute concern from swallowing the visit


Caregivers almost always arrive with a concern. Address it, document it, and if it's significant, bill it as a separate problem-oriented service alongside the preventive visit, but don't let the sick-visit HPI displace the preventive components. If you need structure for the concern itself, a dedicated[HPI template](https://www.sully.ai/resource-hub/hpi) keeps it contained.


**Bottom line:** A complete well-child note answers three questions any reviewer will ask: was every age-indicated component addressed, was each screen done with a named tool and recorded result, and does the age on the date of service match the preventive code billed?


## Common Well-Child Documentation Mistakes to Avoid


Even experienced pediatric clinicians fall into the same traps, especially at fifteen visits a day.


-


**Screenings without scores.** "M-CHAT done, normal" won't survive an audit. Record the instrument and the numeric result every time.


-


**Raw growth numbers without percentiles.** Fix it by charting percentiles and one line of trend interpretation at every visit.


-


**Copy-forward guidance sections.** A 6-month note that still mentions rear-facing car seat "when the time comes" from the 2-month visit reads as boilerplate. Refresh the topics to the visit age.


-


**Missing the confidential adolescent interview.** Document that time alone occurred and that confidentiality limits were explained, keeping sensitive content appropriately protected per your state's minor-consent rules.


-


**Preventive and problem visits blended into one narrative.** When a significant acute issue comes up, document it as a distinct problem with its own assessment and plan so both services are supportable.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What should be included in a well-child visit note?


A complete well-child note includes the visit age, interval history, nutrition and sleep, developmental surveillance with standardized screening at scheduled ages, growth parameters with percentiles, a full physical exam, age-indicated screenings with instruments and results, immunizations with counseling documented, specific anticipatory guidance topics, and an assessment and plan with the return interval.


### What is the Bright Futures periodicity schedule?


It's the AAP's recommended schedule of preventive visits and the components due at each one: which screenings, measurements, and guidance topics belong at every age from newborn through 21 years. Most payers and quality programs benchmark well-child documentation against it, which is why well-child templates are built to follow it.


### How do you document developmental screening?


Name the standardized instrument, record the score or domain results, and state the action taken. For example: "ASQ-3 at 18 months: communication domain in monitoring zone; referral to early intervention placed." Surveillance without a standardized tool should be documented as surveillance, not screening.


### What ages require autism screening?


The AAP recommends standardized autism-specific screening at the 18-month and 24-month visits, most commonly with the M-CHAT-R/F, in addition to general developmental screening at 9, 18, and 30 months. Document the score even when it's negative.


### Is a well-child visit note the same as a SOAP note?


No. A SOAP note is organized around a presenting problem; a well-child note is organized around age-expected preventive components. When an acute concern comes up during a well visit, it's documented as a distinct problem alongside the preventive content rather than restructuring the whole note around it.
